name: Cushion compact

lead: A cushion compact is a makeup case containing a sponge saturated with liquid foundation or BB-style base, applied by dabbing with an included puff. It evens skin tone with a light, dewy finish and is easy to carry and reapply.
The format is associated with Korean beauty, the same market that developed BB cream in the 1980s as a lighter alternative to Western foundation [1]. Many versions advertise SPF.

paras: Users press the puff on the sponge and pat it over the face, building coverage in thin layers and touching up through the day. Refill pads allow reuse of the case. Wear is temporary and removed with cleansing.
Risks are those of cosmetics generally: possible irritation or allergy to ingredients, and bacteria buildup on a shared or unwashed puff. Shade ranges can be limited.

angle.text: It visibly evens tone and covers blemishes while looking light on the skin, and the compact format makes midday touch-ups simple.

lead: A cushion compact is a foundation format in which liquid base makeup is held in a sponge inside a compact and transferred with a puff. For appearance it gives sheer-to-medium, even coverage with a glowy skin finish and can be reapplied on the go.

It descends from the Korean market of light base products. Wikipedia notes that BB cream was developed further in South Korea in the 1980s, that Korean women often use it in place of heavy Western foundations, and that many contain skincare ingredients such as hyaluronic acid.[1] Cushion products extend that preference into a portable compact. Traditional powder compacts date to the early 1900s.[2]
infobox: Compact with liquid-soaked sponge and puff

paras: The product pairs a compact case with a sponge infused with liquid foundation and an applicator puff. It belongs to the Korean base-makeup tradition that includes BB cream, whose coverage is often described as designed to oxidise toward the wearer's tone and to cover and treat blemishes.[1]
Powder compacts date to the early 1900s, when makeup was not widely accepted, and were produced in ornate forms in the Art Deco era.[2]
